stories.title: NASA's Voyager 1 becomes the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth
paragraphs: NASA says its Voyager 1 probe reached one light-day from Earth at 2:16 a.m. PST on Nov. 18, 2026, after more than 49 years of travel. A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours, which NASA puts at about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). According to the agency, Voyager team members at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took the spacecraft's radio transmission, traveling at the speed of light, to reach Earth. The Conversation notes that no human-built object of any kind had reached that distance before.

NASA says the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14. The spacecraft is still transmitting a basic radio carrier wave that normally conveys that data, and NASA says mission engineers used it, plus trajectory calculations, to confirm the milestone while they continue to analyze the data issue. Space.com, quoting a JPL representative, also points to a roughly 48-hour period last month in which Voyager 1 stopped responding to commands before it recovered.

NASA says both probes lose about 4 watts of power each year as their plutonium supply decays, and that an energy-saving effort this year is expected to keep their current science instruments running until at least their 50th launch anniversaries. "We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said in NASA's release.

image.alt: Artist's concept of NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft in interstellar space

stories.title: A brain region known for understanding speech also helps start every spoken word, study finds
paragraphs: A study published Nov. 19, 2026, in the journal Science finds that a small part of Wernicke's area, a brain region long known for helping people understand speech, also plays a key role in producing it, Science News and Live Science report. The spot is the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, just above the left ear. "Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it," Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing quoted by Science News.

According to Live Science, the team recorded brain activity in 28 people with epilepsy who already had electrodes implanted, and found a small group of cells that fired about a quarter of a second before participants spoke. The researchers also mapped the brains of hundreds of people having temporal-lobe tumors removed and found that patients were much more likely to have trouble speaking if surgery damaged Wernicke's area. In 13 people, electrical stimulation of the spot just before speaking caused word errors resembling Wernicke's aphasia.

The researchers also decoded what two volunteers with paralysis were attempting to say by monitoring neurons in this area through implanted electrodes, Live Science reports. UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva told Science News that the region could be an additional target for speech-restoring brain implants, which have mostly focused on the motor cortex.

Neurologist Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin, quoted by Science News, called the study convincing evidence that the spot is critical for speech production. "We already knew that damage to Wernicke's area can lead to speech production errors, but this publication answers why," New York University neuroscientist Adeen Flinker, who was not involved, told Live Science.

image.alt: Brain diagram highlighting Wernicke's area and the left posterior superior temporal gyrus

stories.title: Engine trouble ends Hayabusa2's planned asteroid landing; JAXA switches to a 2028 flyby
paragraphs: Japan's space agency JAXA has dropped its plan for the Hayabusa2 spacecraft to rendezvous with and attempt to land on the small near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031, Space.com reported on Nov. 19, 2026. According to Space.com, the spacecraft will instead make a high-speed flyby of another tiny asteroid, 2015 BM510, in April 2028, with no landing.

Space.com reports that JAXA announced the decision at a press conference on Nov. 17, a day after a Cabinet Office space policy subcommittee meeting. According to JAXA officials cited by Space.com, the last working thruster of Hayabusa2's four ion engines malfunctioned in mid-August, and a sensor detected unexpected erosion of the spacecraft's surface. "The deterioration of the onboard equipment ... is becoming increasingly evident," extended-mission team leader Yuya Mimasu said, as quoted by the Japan Times and reported by Space.com.

Hayabusa2 launched in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu and delivered those samples to Earth in December 2020 in a reentry capsule, according to Space.com. Since then it has flown an extended mission, including a close flyby of the asteroid Torifune in July. Space.com reports that scientists describe 2015 BM510 as a D-type asteroid, thought to be organic-rich and comet-like, and that it is also the primary target of a proposal for the European Space Agency's mini-Fast mission series.

image.alt: Artist's depiction of Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft passing near Earth

stories.title: Rubin Observatory finds two ancient Trojan asteroids trailing Neptune, the first new ones in that swarm in 15 years
paragraphs: Astronomers using the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory have confirmed two new long-term stable Trojan asteroids in Neptune's trailing (L5) swarm and identified a third object as a candidate, Live Science reported on Nov. 19, 2026. The findings were published Oct. 15 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by a team led by Meg Schwamb of Queen's University Belfast. Earth.com reports that the two confirmed objects, 2025 MH348 and 2025 NN80, double the list of trailing Trojans known to be on orbits stable for billions of years from two to four, and that a third object, 2025 MD138, remains a candidate.

Trojan asteroids share a planet's orbit around the sun, gathering about 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet, where the pulls of the sun and the planet balance, Live Science explains. The researchers told Live Science that Neptune's trailing Trojans have been hard to find because they are extremely faint and, for nearly 15 years, sat in front of the crowded central region of the Milky Way. Since 2025 that part of the sky has slowly moved away from the galactic plane, and Rubin's early Science Validation Survey happened to cover it, finding the objects within three weeks of the survey's start.

Computer models of the orbits showed the two confirmed objects will keep trailing Neptune for a billion years, which Live Science reports suggests their paths may date back to the early solar system. The third object stayed stable in only some simulations, so it is listed as a candidate. The simulations also showed highly tilted orbits, like those of the previously known L5 Trojans, suggesting Neptune captured them rather than forming alongside them, according to Live Science.

According to Earth.com, 2025 MH348 and the candidate were first detected on June 21, 2025, one day after the test survey began, and 2025 NN80 on July 7; older Pan-STARRS1 detections later extended their observed orbits. Phys.org, citing a Queen's University Belfast release, reports that Rubin's images in different filters let the team show that Neptune's leading and trailing Trojans have similar surfaces, and that Rubin's survey is expected to find tens to hundreds of Neptune Trojans in both groups.

image.alt: Artist's rendition of Trojan asteroids trailing Neptune
